title: Feminist IR

cards.h: Where are the women in world politics?
cards.b: Feminist IR began as a simple question by Cynthia Enloe: 'Where are the women?' Traditional IR studies states, wars and markets, yet gender shapes all three. The approach is now a regular Paper II topic, with the Women, Peace and Security agenda, and Indian examples.
Sex is biological; gender is the social meaning of masculinity and femininity, which is unequal.
Tickner's Gender in International Relations (1992) re-reads Morgenthau's six principles as masculine.

cards.h: Enloe and the personal as international
cards.b:
In Bananas, Beaches and Bases (1989) Cynthia Enloe shows how women's labour, domestic work, military wives, sex workers and diplomatic spouses support international politics. 'The personal is international'. Her method: follow women through supply chains and bases to see hidden power.

Keep the name, the year and the one-line claim ready. These three details are what examiners look for when they check a concept.

Feminists redefine security: not just the state's borders, but safety at home and in society. They study sexual violence as a weapon of war (Bosnia and Rwanda in the 1990s, the Rome Statute 1998), militarised masculinity, and women as combatants and peace-builders. Carol Cohn's 'Sex and Death in the Rational World of Defense Intellectuals' (1987) shows how nuclear strategy talk is gendered.

UN Security Council Resolution 1325 (2000) urged women's participation in peace processes and protection from violence. It was followed by later resolutions (1820, 2122 and others), and many states made National Action Plans. Research (for example by UN Women) suggests peace agreements are likelier to last when women take part.

Sweden declared a feminist foreign policy in 2014; Canada, France, Mexico and others followed with feminist aid or diplomacy. Sweden dropped the label in 2022 after a change of government; several others have scaled back since, so treat this as contested. Three Rs: rights, representation, resources.

• Mainstream realists: gender is not central to state behaviour.
  • Essentialism: assuming women are naturally peaceful.
  • Western feminism may ignore the voices of Southern women (Mohanty).
  • Hard to test empirically.
  • Defenders: it widens the questions IR can ask.

In an answer, give two points for and two against, then close with a balanced verdict. Examiners reward a clear stand backed by a named thinker or case.

Gandhi linked non-violence with women's strength. India sent the first all-women Formed Police Unit to a UN mission, in Liberia in 2007. The Supreme Court (Babita Puniya, 2020) allowed permanent commission for women in the Army, and Parliament passed the 106th Amendment (2023). Critics note that India has not adopted a formal National Action Plan on 1325 (verify current status).

"Explain how feminist approaches challenge mainstream IR."
"Examine the Women, Peace and Security agenda."
"Is a feminist foreign policy possible and desirable?"

Structure: problem, gender concept, schools, Enloe and Tickner, security, UNSCR 1325, critique, India.

Marks tip: open with a one-line definition, use two or three named thinkers, cases or Articles, add one Indian example, and end with a balanced, forward-looking line. Keep within the word limit.
